## CIRCT continues MLIR toward hardware {#circt-continuation}

[CIRCT](https://circt.llvm.org/) adds representations and transformations for
the lower part of the abstraction stack.

| Level | What the IR must make explicit |
|---|---|
| numerical intent | operations, types, and mathematical semantics |
| hardware architecture | resources, communication, and scheduling |
| RTL | modules, combinational logic, state, and clocks |
| implementation | gates, cells, placement, and wires |

::: {.fragment}
It is not one hardware IR. It is a set of **dialects that preserve useful
decisions at different levels**.
:::

## The examples have direct CIRCT vocabulary {#circt-dialects}

| SystemVerilog example | CIRCT vocabulary | Preserved meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `module mul_add4` | [`hw.module`](https://circt.llvm.org/docs/Dialects/HW/) | module boundary and ports |
| `mul4 u_mul (...)` | `hw.instance` | one elaborated hardware instance |
| `assign product = a * b` | [`comb.mul`](https://circt.llvm.org/docs/Dialects/Comb/) | typed combinational dataflow |
| `always_ff @(posedge clk)` | [`seq.compreg`](https://circt.llvm.org/docs/Dialects/Seq/) | clocked state |

::: {.fragment}
Passes can now ask the primer's questions directly: **what is structural, what
is combinational, and what crosses a clock edge?**
:::

## One multiplier, two ways into CIRCT {#circt-two-entrances .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**A complete architecture in SystemVerilog**

```systemverilog
module e4m3fn_mul(
  input  logic [7:0] lhs, rhs,
  output logic [7:0] result
);
  // Decode fields.
  // Multiply significands.
  // Normalize and round.
  // Pack zeros, subnormals and NaNs.
endmodule
```

`circt-verilog` imports the decisions already present in the RTL.
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
**The numerical operation in `arith`**

```mlir
hw.module @e4m3fn_mul(
    in %lhs : i8, in %rhs : i8,
    out result : i8) {
  %lhsf = arith.bitcast %lhs
      : i8 to f8E4M3FN
  %rhsf = arith.bitcast %rhs
      : i8 to f8E4M3FN
  %product = arith.mulf %lhsf, %rhsf
      : f8E4M3FN
  %result = arith.bitcast %product
      : f8E4M3FN to i8
  hw.output %result : i8
}
```
:::
::::

## Importing RTL exposes the architecture {#circt-imported-datapath .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```mlir
%lhsExp = comb.extract %lhs from 3
    : (i8) -> i4
%lhsFrac = comb.extract %lhs from 0
    : (i8) -> i3
%lhsSign = comb.extract %lhs from 7
    : (i8) -> i1

%resultSign = comb.xor %lhsSign, %rhsSign : i1
%lhsSig = comb.concat %zero4, %lhsNormal,
    %lhsFrac : i4, i1, i3
%rhsSig = comb.concat %zero4, %rhsNormal,
    %rhsFrac : i4, i1, i3
%sigProduct = comb.mul %lhsSig, %rhsSig : i8
```
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.incremental}
- `hw.module` preserves the eight-bit interface.

- `comb.extract` gives names to the packed fields.

- `comb.mul` is now a **four-bit significand multiplier**, not a floating-point
  operation.

- Muxes and comparisons make exceptional behavior structural.
:::
:::
::::

## Floating-point multiplication is a datapath {#circt-multiplier-parts}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="59%"}
![](assets/images/digital-design/yosys/e4m3_mul_parts.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Word-level schematic separating sign, exponent, and significand paths of an E4M3 multiplier" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="41%"}
::: {.incremental}
1. **Decode** sign, exponent, fraction, zero, and NaN.

2. **Multiply** the four-bit significands.

3. **Normalize** the eight-bit product.

4. **Round** back to three fraction bits.

5. **Select and pack** the final E4M3 encoding.
:::
:::
::::

## State and control retain their own structure {#circt-state-control .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**A register is not an arithmetic operation**

```mlir
%product = comb.mul %a, %b : i8
%product_q = seq.compreg %product, %clk : i8
```

`seq` records that a value exists **after a clock edge**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**A controller can remain an FSM**

```mlir
fsm.state @idle transitions {
  fsm.transition @run guard {
    fsm.return %start
  }
}
fsm.state @run transitions {
  fsm.transition @idle
}
```

`fsm` preserves states and transitions until lowering them is useful.
:::
::::

## Lowering is where intent becomes a circuit {#circt-lowering-decision}

::: {.incremental}
- `arith.mulf` says **what numerical operation** must be preserved.

- `hw` and `comb` say **which bit-vector network** implements it.

- `seq` says **when values are available**.

- Synthesis decides **which gates or LUTs** realize the network.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The tutorial will traverse those views in one direction, prove that they agree,
then return to `arith.mulf` to write our own lowering.
:::
